name: IBM Roadmap Revisions
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Reading Between the Lines of IBM's Own Roadmap
lesson.summary: IBM has published detailed, dated, public technical roadmaps for its quantum program since 2020, which makes it one of the only quantum computing companies whose own predictions can be checked against its own later revisions, and those revisions tell a candid story.
lesson.body:
Most companies in the catalog of broken promises made informal predictions in interviews, conference talks, or marketing copy, which makes them hard to pin down precisely. IBM is unusual in the field for publishing an actual dated, versioned public roadmap for its quantum computing hardware and software, updated and reissued periodically since 2020. This is, in one sense, an admirable level of transparency, since it lets outside observers check IBM's own past predictions against what it later delivered, rather than relying on secondhand reporting. It also means IBM's roadmap revisions are unusually well documented evidence of the timeline pattern discussed throughout this unit.

The chip lineage itself tells part of the story. Eagle, released in 2021 with 127 qubits, and Condor, released in 2023 with a reported 1,121 qubits, represented one strategic direction: scale the number of physical qubits on a single chip as far as possible. But as the earlier chapter on the 1,121-qubit chip described, IBM's own 2023 announcement pivoted its emphasis toward a different chip, Heron, with far fewer qubits but meaningfully better error rates, and toward a modular strategy of linking multiple mid-sized chips rather than continuing to build single enormous ones. That pivot is itself a roadmap revision: the qubit-scaling strategy implied by the 2020 and 2021 roadmap language was quietly de-emphasized once Condor demonstrated that scaling qubit count alone was running into diminishing returns.

IBM's stated timelines for fault-tolerant, error-corrected quantum computing have moved as well. Roadmap materials issued around 2020 and 2021 described paths toward large-scale, error-corrected systems on timelines that, read in hindsight, were optimistic relative to what the 2023 and later roadmap versions described. Later roadmap versions pushed specific fault-tolerance milestones further out and added more intermediate steps, including new error-mitigation techniques meant to extract more useful computation out of NISQ-era hardware while true error correction remained further away than earlier materials had implied. This is precisely the three-to-five-year pattern described earlier in this unit, playing out inside a single company's own sequential planning documents rather than across different companies or decades.

It would be unfair to describe this as IBM simply failing to deliver. Compared to competitors, IBM has been unusually willing to publish specific, checkable commitments in the first place, which is what makes the revisions visible and analyzable at all. A company that never states a specific timeline can never be caught missing one. IBM's willingness to be concrete, and to revise those specifics candidly as new information about the engineering came in, is arguably closer to good scientific practice than the vaguer, less falsifiable claims common elsewhere in the industry.

The lesson for evaluating any hardware company's roadmap, IBM's included, is to treat published roadmaps as living hypotheses rather than commitments, and to watch specifically for the direction revisions move in. Revisions that push timelines later while adding technical detail, as IBM's have generally done, suggest a company learning from real engineering setbacks and communicating them, which is a healthier pattern than the vaguer, non-falsifiable optimism found in the startup pitches and consultant reports covered in the next two chapters.
